title: MLOps & CI/CD for ML
blurb: Tests why ML pipelines gate on code, data and model, the registry as the central object, data validation, performance gates that compare against production, training-serving skew, and choosing between blue-green, canary, shadow and rolling deploys.

questions.prompt: Which questions does the chapter say ML CI/CD has to ask at each gate? Select all that apply.
options: Is the model still good enough, compared with production?
Is the model the most sophisticated algorithm available?
Does the code still work?
Is the data still valid?
questions.explanation: Regular CI/CD asks only the first. ML adds data validity and model quality, because code, data and model parameters can all change. The chapter's worked example shows the gate does not care how sophisticated an algorithm is, only whether the number went up.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs only unit tests on the training code. What can it ship without noticing?
options: Only models that are better than production, so nothing bad can ship
A model trained on corrupted data, or one worse than the live model
Nothing, since correct code always gives a correct model
Only models with syntax errors, which the unit tests miss
questions.explanation: The chapter says a pipeline checking only code correctness will happily ship a model trained on corrupted data, or one that is technically deployable but worse than what is live. Correct code does not guarantee a good model, because the data and parameters also change.

questions.prompt: In Procedure 24.1, what does archive_existing_versions=True prevent?
options: A new version being registered without metrics
Two versions marked Production at once
Old versions being deleted from storage
The model being logged without a signature
questions.explanation: The flag archives the previous Production version during the transition. Without it, two versions can be Production at the same time, which defeats the point of one answer to "what's live?". Archiving keeps old versions, it does not delete them.

questions.prompt: What does each registered model version carry, per the chapter?
options: A copy of the serving container, so it can deploy without a build
Its metrics, the code commit and data version that produced it, and a stage
The full training data, so the version can be retrained offline
Only the model file itself, with the metrics kept on a separate tracking server
questions.explanation: Each version is registered with its metrics, its code commit and data version, and a stage. That is what turns "which model is live?" into a query. The registry does not store the training data or a container.

refLinks.label: §24.2.1 The Model Registry as the Central Object

questions.prompt: What is training-serving skew?
options: The serving machine is slower than the training machine.
Training and serving code transform features differently.
Training uses a newer library version than the registry.
The model is trained on far more data than it will ever see in production traffic.
questions.explanation: Skew is when the two code paths transform features even slightly differently. The model looks good in evaluation and does badly live. The fix is one shared, versioned feature pipeline used by both, never two reimplementations.

refLinks.label: §24.2.2 CI for ML: What Gets Tested

questions.prompt: Where should data validation run, per Procedure 24.2?
options: After training, alongside the performance gate
After deployment, as part of monitoring
Only when a training run fails
First, before any row is used to fit anything
questions.explanation: The procedure says data validation is the first stage, before a single row is used. It catches upstream breakages before they silently degrade a retrained model. Running it after training is too late to stop that.

questions.prompt: validate_data in Listing 24.2 is called with max_null_rate=0.01. One expected column is 3% null and the rest are complete. What does it return?
options: (False, ["Null rate exceeds threshold"])
(False, ["Missing columns"])
(True, ["Null rate exceeds threshold"])
(True, []), because the average null rate across columns is under 1%
questions.explanation: The check takes isnull().mean() per column, then .max(). The worst column is 0.03 > 0.01, so the error is added and the function returns len(errors) == 0, which is False, with that one error. It checks the worst column, not the average.

questions.prompt: Which of these are integration tests for the serving pipeline, as the chapter describes them? Select all that apply.
options: Does the serialised model load?
Does the API return the expected schema?
Is the candidate's F1 above the production model's?
Does it survive a malformed request without crashing?
questions.explanation: Integration tests check the code path, separate from model quality. Comparing F1 with production is the model performance regression test, a different kind of check.

refLinks.label: §24.2.2 CI for ML: What Gets Tested

questions.prompt: A model scores well in offline evaluation but badly in production. The training notebook scales income with a StandardScaler. The serving code divides income by a hard-coded constant someone wrote down. What does the chapter prescribe?
options: One shared, versioned preprocessing pipeline used by both training and serving
A canary deploy, so the skew only affects a few users
Retraining the model more often, so it adapts to the serving transform
A second test set drawn from production data, so offline evaluation matches serving
questions.explanation: This is training-serving skew. The chapter's fix is a single shared pipeline (Chapter 14's sklearn.Pipeline pattern) used by both paths. A canary limits damage but does not remove the bug. Retraining does not help, because training still uses the other transform.

questions.prompt: What two conditions does the performance gate in Procedure 24.3 check?
options: The candidate clears a fixed minimum, and it is not worse than the production model
The candidate has more parameters than the production model, and clears a fixed minimum
The candidate clears a fixed minimum, and it trains faster than production
The candidate is better than production by at least 5%, and its data is valid
questions.explanation: gate_candidate checks candidate_f1 >= min_f1 and that candidate_f1 is not below production_f1 minus a tolerance. Data validity is a separate test, and size and speed are not in the gate.

questions.prompt: gate_candidate(candidate_f1=0.81, production_f1=0.83, min_f1=0.5, tolerance=0.0). What happens?
options: It passes, because 0.81 is well above the minimum of 0.5.
It fails with two reasons, below minimum and a regression.
It passes, because the gap is under the tolerance.
It fails with one reason, a regression against production.
questions.explanation: 0.81 clears 0.5, so there is no minimum failure. 0.81 < 0.83 − 0.0, so regressed is True and one reason is added. The function returns False with that single reason.

questions.prompt: The production model has F1 = 0.9722. With min_f1 = 0.5, what is the smallest tolerance that would let the Gradient Boosting candidate (F1 = 0.9660) pass? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The candidate fails while 0.9660 < 0.9722 − tolerance. It passes once tolerance ≥ 0.9722 − 0.9660 = 0.0062. Setting a tolerance means accepting a small drop on purpose.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why do all three candidates fail the gate even though each has F1 above 0.95?
options: Tree models are not allowed to replace a linear model that is already in the registry.
Their data failed validation, so the gate never evaluated them.
Each scores below the production model's 0.9722, so the regression check fails.
Each falls below the absolute minimum, which was set at 0.97.
questions.explanation: The minimum was 0.5, so every candidate cleared it. They fail because 0.9510, 0.9583 and 0.9660 are all below 0.9722. An absolute-only gate would have shipped the Gradient Boosting candidate as a downgrade. The gate doesn't care which algorithm is used.

questions.prompt: After the worked example, a teammate proposes trying a neural network next, because it is more advanced. What does the chapter say would clear this bar?
options: Removing the production comparison, since the baseline is unusually strong.
Better tuning against this baseline, such as hyperparameter search or stacking.
Any more advanced algorithm, because sophistication tends to win on tabular data.
Lowering min_f1, because the absolute bar is what blocks the candidates.
questions.explanation: The chapter says getting past this bar needs better tuning (Chapter 17) or stacking (Chapter 12) aimed at this baseline, not a fancier-sounding algorithm. The absolute bar is not what blocks them. Removing the comparison is how silent regressions ship.

questions.prompt: Which strategy sends the new model a copy of live traffic and logs its predictions without serving them?
options: Blue-green switch-over
Shadow (dark launch)
Canary release
Rolling update
questions.explanation: Shadow mirrors traffic to the new model and never shows its output to users. That is zero production risk, but it checks prediction quality only, not business impact. Canary serves real users a small share. Blue-green switches all at once. Rolling updates instances one by one.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of blue-green deployment?
options: It needs a copy of production traffic, which doubles the cost of every request.
Rollback is slow, because the old model is torn down first.
All traffic switches at once, so there is no gradual signal before the switch.
It can only update one instance at a time.
questions.explanation: Blue-green runs both versions and switches everything at once. Rollback is fast, because the old version is still there, but you get no gradual signal. Mirroring traffic is shadow, and one instance at a time is rolling.

questions.prompt: What can a shadow deployment not tell you about a new fraud model?
options: Its business impact, since no user ever acts on what it predicts
Whether its predictions agree with those of the current production model
How its predictions are distributed on real inputs
Whether it runs without errors on live traffic
questions.explanation: Shadow logs predictions on real traffic, so you can compare outputs, catch errors and see distributions. Because nothing it predicts is served, you can't see the effect on blocked fraud, customer friction or revenue. The chapter says shadow validates prediction quality only.

questions.prompt: Two teams ship models next week: a product-recommendation engine and a medical-triage classifier. Which plan fits the chapter's rule that strategy scales with the cost of a bad prediction?
options: Shadow for recommendations, and blue-green for triage
Blue-green for both, because rollback is fastest
Canary for both, because it catches problems before everyone is affected
Canary for recommendations, and shadow validation first for triage
questions.explanation: The chapter says a recommendation engine can tolerate canary, while a fraud or medical-triage model often needs shadow validation first. A canary on triage exposes real patients to an untested model, even if only a few. Blue-green gives no gradual signal at all.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say a notebook is a bad place to run production training?
options: Notebooks can't save models to the registry.
Cells run out of order, state is hidden, and schedulers can't easily run it on a timer.
Notebooks can't import sklearn or MLflow.
Notebooks always use more memory and CPU than the same code run as a script.
questions.explanation: The chapter keeps notebooks for development and moves production training into a versioned script with load_data, build_pipeline, train, evaluate and main. That runs the same for a human, CI or a scheduler, and can be unit-tested and reviewed. Notebooks can import libraries and log to MLflow.

questions.prompt: Which level of pipeline does the chapter's table recommend for most production teams?
options: CI tests on code and data only
No pipeline, with manual retraining
CI tests plus a model performance gate
Full CI/CD with canary or shadow deploys
questions.explanation: The table marks "CI + model performance gate" as best for most production teams. It catches code bugs, schema breaks and silent quality regressions. Full CI/CD with canary or shadow is for high-stakes or high-traffic models.

questions.prompt: What should set how much a team invests in its ML pipeline, per the chapter?
options: How expensive a bad model in production would be
Whether the team uses SageMaker
The number of models already registered in the registry
The size of the team
questions.explanation: The chapter says the right investment scales with the cost of a bad model in production, not with team size alone. A one-person team running a medical model needs more than a large team running a toy recommender.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter separate MLOps from experiment tracking?
options: MLOps logs runs for people to compare. Tracking automates the promotion decision.
Tracking is for production. MLOps is for prototypes.
Tracking records runs for people to compare. MLOps automates promotion from those records.
They are the same practice under two names.
questions.explanation: The chapter says tracking is necessary but not sufficient for MLOps. Tracking records what happened. MLOps turns that record into automated gates and deploys.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why an ML CI pipeline needs to check three things (code, data, model quality) where a traditional software CI pipeline only needs to check one.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Traditional software only has code that changes between releases. The same input always produces the same output for a given code version, so checking "does the code still work" (tests passing) is sufficient. ML systems have code, data, and learned parameters all changing independently. The same code can produce a worse model if the training data shifts, or if hyperparameters change, neither of which a code-only test suite would catch. That's why data validity and model quality need their own separate checks.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the deployment strategy best suited to a fraud model where a bad prediction is very costly and real-traffic validation is needed before any user is affected.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Shadow deployment. It validates the new model against real production traffic patterns while producing zero risk to actual users, since predictions are only logged, never served. That makes it the right choice before any user is exposed to a costly-if-wrong fraud model's decisions.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 24.4's measured results, explain specifically why the Gradient Boosting candidate (F1=0.9660) would have passed a gate that only checked `candidate_f1 >= 0.5`, and why Procedure 24.3's actual gate correctly rejected it anyway.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A gate checking only `candidate_f1 >= 0.5` would pass the Gradient Boosting candidate outright, since 0.9660 comfortably clears 0.5. Procedure 24.3's actual gate adds the second condition: comparing against the current production metric (0.9722). 0.9660 is below 0.9722, so the "regression vs. production" check fires and correctly rejects it despite easily clearing the absolute bar.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 24.3's gate function, compute the result of `gate_candidate(0.9660, 0.9722, min_f1=0.5, tolerance=0.01)`. Does adding a 0.01 tolerance change the outcome for the Gradient Boosting candidate from this chapter's Worked Example?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `gate_candidate(0.9660, 0.9722, min_f1=0.5, tolerance=0.01)`: the absolute check passes (0.9660 ≥ 0.5). The regression check compares $0.9660$ against $0.9722 - 0.01 = 0.9612$. Since $0.9660 \geq 0.9612$, no regression is flagged either. With a 0.01 tolerance, the Gradient Boosting candidate **would pass**. A small tolerance band is enough to let a candidate through that's marginally, but not meaningfully, below the incumbent. This illustrates why the tolerance parameter itself is a real design decision, not just a technicality.

bookExercises.prompt: A team's gate always reports "candidate passed" even when a teammate can see in the logs that the new model's F1 is clearly worse. Using this chapter's Troubleshooting-style reasoning, name the most likely bug in how the gate is implemented.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The most likely bug is the gate comparing against a stale, cached production metric captured at pipeline-definition time, rather than querying the registry live at gate-check time. If the "production" number used in the comparison was hardcoded or fetched once and never refreshed, a genuinely worse candidate could pass simply because it's being compared against an outdated (possibly already-superseded or incorrect) baseline number instead of the actual current production metric.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer says "we already have MLflow tracking every run, so we have MLOps." Using this chapter's How This Connects section, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Tracking every run gives you the logging and comparison half of the picture. You can see what was tried. But MLOps is specifically about *automating* the promotion and deployment decision based on that logged data. Does a new model get gated, tested, and shipped automatically, or does someone still manually decide and push it? Tracking is necessary but not sufficient. Without the gate and pipeline automation this chapter covers, you still have the exact failure mode from the Motivation: a manually-pushed regression that nobody caught."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Sculley et al. "Continuous Delivery for Machine Learning" piece's discussion of shadow deployment. Identify the specific limitation it names for shadow mode, and relate it to why this chapter recommends canary as the more common default for most production ML services.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Shadow deployment's named limitation is that it validates prediction quality but not real-world business impact. Since shadow predictions are never actually served to users, there's no way to observe how the new model's decisions would have changed user behaviour, conversion, or other downstream business metrics that only manifest when real users actually see and react to the new model's outputs. Canary is recommended as the more common default specifically because it exposes the new model to a small slice of *real* consequences, catching business-impact problems shadow mode structurally cannot detect, while still limiting the blast radius if something goes wrong.
